item.title: RMB Latitudes 2026 | Nigeria Focus
item.description: RMB Latitudes 2026 Presents Nigeria Focus Each year, RMB Latitudes Art Fair spotlights one African country through its International Focus programme, fostering exchange and visibility across the continent. In 2026, the programme turns to Nigeria, bringing together more than 30 artists working across painting, photography, textile and sculpture. As one of the most expansive presentations of contemporary Nigerian practice within a cross-continental framework, Nigeria Focus reflects a breadth of voices and approaches rarely brought together between West and Southern Africa. Nigeria Focus unfolds as a cross-border exhibition, beginning in Lagos (15 April 2026) and culminating at RMB Latitudes Art Fair in Johannesburg (22–24 May 2026). The Lagos presentation offers a curated preview of selected artists, situating the works within their local context before the full exhibition is presented in Johannesburg, connecting audiences, collectors and institutions across West and Southern Africa. item.title: Notes from the Fire
item.description: In a world defined by acceleration and consumption, what does it mean to leave a mark? Notes from the Fire is a multidisciplinary solo exhibition by Givan Lötz. Presenting work of visual speculative fiction, Lötz imagines a time after time. Wax, casting, and surface serve as residues of a world forged in fire — an enduring imprint of heat, loss, and survival. Set within the speculative era of the Pyrocene, the exhibition unfolds as a fragmented archive of the future. Carbonised artefacts, coded surfaces, and partial systems speak to a reality in which knowledge is no longer stable, and meaning must be excavated rather than consumed. With surfaces cryptic and functions opaque, Notes from the Fire invites reflection and curiosity from its audience, presenting traces of a world disturbingly familiar yet wonderfully strange. The exhibition gestures toward the urgency of climate collapse driven by human consequences, while resisting complete moral closure and resolution. Instead, it holds space for endurance where something stubbornly human remains: the impulse to mark, to remember, to leave a signal in the ashes.

item.title: Above and Beyond
item.description: RMB Latitudes Art Fair presents a Special Project by featured artist Dada Khanyisa (b. 1991, Umzimkhulu; lives in Cape Town). Titled Above and Beyond, the exhibition is positioned in one of the Fair's most distinctive architectural spaces, the Turret. Khanyisa's practice centres on sculptural paintings and painted wooden assemblages that move between painting, collage and low-relief sculpture. Drawing from everyday social moments and contemporary South African life, Khanyisa transforms intimate interactions into reflections on broader dynamics – from youth culture to community and belonging. The particular site specific installation, comprised of a number of different panels, draws on pop cultural references and memories particular to a young Black adult navigating leisure in Cape Town, Southj Africa. Rendered in the midst of tensions and passion, Khanyisa liberates their figures from the typical idylic stillness of the fine art subject.

item.title: INDEX: INDEPENDENT ARTIST EXHIBITION presented by National Arts Council
item.description: RMB Latitudes Art Fair is pleased to announce a new partnership with the National Arts Council of South Africa (NAC) for the 2026 edition of INDEX is the fair’s platform dedicated to independent and emerging artistic practices. This collaboration marks a considered shift in how public arts funding might more directly intersect with the structures of the contemporary art market. The partnership between INDEX and the NAC proposes a progressive model for aligning institutional support with tangible, market-facing opportunities for artists. Moving beyond traditional funding models, the partnership introduces a sophisticated curatorial approach led by the Latitudes team. Through a cohesive and intentional strategy, the initiative ensures that artworks presented are both narratively compelling and commercially viable. Presented within the broader framework of RMB Latitudes, INDEX 2026 will bring together a dynamic selection of emerging artists from across the continent. The exhibition will feature both a curated presentation shaped within the Latitudes programme, alongside artists identified through the NAC’s open call process — creating a layered and inclusive platform for discovery. Participating artists will benefit from visibility across both the physical fair and Latitudes Online, ensuring engagement with local and international audiences, as well as continued exposure beyond the fair itself. The collaboration further stands as a testament to the NAC’s mandate to support, promote, and develop South Africa’s vibrant arts sector. Through the INDEX 2026 platform, the Council is actively working to dismantle barriers to entry and broaden access for diverse artistic voices.

item.title: ESSAY: Jan Neethling & Robert Hodgins On Friendship and Form
item.description: Each year, ESSAY presents focused dialogues between South African artists across generations, exploring lineage, influence, memory, and material thinking. The programme brings practices into conversation that are not often seen together, offering new perspectives on both established and under-recognised figures. The 2026 edition centres on the work of Jan Neethling, presented in dialogue with a focused selection of works by his former teacher and lifelong friend, Robert Hodgins. Bringing their practices into close proximity, the exhibition considers how influence unfolds over time - shaped as much by friendship, critique, and exchange as by individual artistic trajectories. Neethling’s paintings are marked by restless figuration and shifting, unstable terrains, where portraiture, still-life, and landscape collapse into dense, psychologically charged compositions. Like Hodgins, he draws from observation of people, power, and the world as it presents itself, allowing images to emerge through process rather than prescription. On Friendship and Form foregrounds a relationship sustained over decades. In this space, painting becomes a site of exchange - where influence is not fixed, but continually negotiated, and where two distinct practices remain deeply, and productively, intertwined

item.title: Real Heroes
item.description: Photographic series by Clint Strydom Real Heroes, the acclaimed photographic series by Clint Strydom, continues to resonate as a celebration of football in its most authentic form. At a time when the global game captures the world’s attention with the Football World cup 2026 taking place in the United States, Canada and Mexica this year, these photographs remind us that the true power of football lies not only in the stadiums of international competition, but in the countless children who play simply for the love of it. Football is often told through the spectacle of the professional game, packed stadiums, global superstars, and the theatre of international tournaments. But beyond the floodlights and television cameras lies another story, one that unfolds daily on beaches, dusty township grounds, and improvised fields across South Africa. In Real Heroes, photographer Clint Strydom turns his lens toward these quieter moments of the game. The series captures children playing football with an intensity and joy that exists far from the world’s arenas. With worn balls, makeshift goals, and limitless imagination, they play simply for the love of the game. Through these photographs, Strydom sought to share the stories of South African children who embody football’s purest spirit. Their matches unfold on stretches of sand, in open fields, and between township streets where the boundaries of the pitch are defined by whatever the environment provides. Here, football is not spectacle or industry; it is community, expression, and belonging. Most of the images are rendered in striking black and white. This choice strips away distraction and focuses attention on form, motion, and emotion. Light and shadow carve silhouettes of bodies leaping through the air; the textures of sand, dust, and sky become part of the visual rhythm of the game. Each frame captures a fleeting moment of movement, a child suspended mid-kick, a ball barely intact, the improvisation of play against vast South African landscapes. What emerges is a portrait of resilience and creativity. The children in these photographs often play with minimal resources, yet their commitment to the game is unwavering. Their ingenuity, determination, and joy transform ordinary spaces into places of possibility. Strydom approaches his subjects with empathy and respect. Rather than presenting them as distant observers of the global game, he photographs them as protagonists in their own right, young players whose passion mirrors that of any professional athlete. In this sense, they are the true heroes of football. The landscapes themselves, sweeping coastlines, expansive skies, and gritty township grounds, are inseparable from the identity of the game in South Africa. Football here is deeply tied to place and community, shaped by the rhythms of everyday life. Through Real Heroes, Strydom invites viewers to reconsider where the heart of football truly lives. Away from the grand arenas and international spotlight, it thrives in the joy of children who gather wherever space allows, carrying the spirit of the game forward with every kick of the ball. The stark visual language of Real Heroes mirrors the environments in which these games unfold. Many of the children play with very little, worn balls, improvised goals, and open ground shaped by sand, dust, and sky. Against this reality, Clint Strydom employs a deliberately exposed photographic technique, using high contrast and dramatic light to strip the images down to their essential elements. The resulting black-and-white compositions emphasize gesture, movement, and emotion. Figures appear almost sculptural against expansive landscapes, while the textures of sand and air become part of the visual rhythm of the game. This starkness does not diminish the scenes; rather, it honors the simplicity and purity of the children’s passion for soccer. Through this approach, Strydom transforms ordinary moments of play into powerful visual studies. The contrast between the children’s limited resources and the expressive energy of their movement reveals a deeper truth: that the spirit of the game lives not in spectacle, but in the raw joy and determination of those who play it.

item.title: Residues of Proximity: ONE BODY, MANY PARTS
item.description: Bag Factory is pleased to present Residues of Proximity: One Body, Many Parts, A solo exhibition by Mosa Anita Kaiser Curated by Melusi Masike This exhibition is a product of the Young/Unframed 2026 programme. This exhibition is a poetic gesture, not of geographic distance but of bodily experience. It approaches the body as both an archival site and a site of seeing. A repository of retrieval, belonging, memory, and internal exile. Internal exile is understood here as a condition of cultural amputation, disjuncture, and disorientation, where one's relationship to memory, place, and cultural experience becomes fractured yet remains present in embodied forms. The exhibition unfolds through motifs drawn from everyday life, becoming a canvas of what was, what remains, and what is continually being remembered. It inhabits the space between the ordinary and the extraordinary, offering a quotidian rapture through acts of reenactment, reflection, and return. Vivid hues and gestures of delight coexist with ghostly underpinnings of sorrow, pain, amputation, and repair. These tensions leave traces of systemic erasure while revealing the resilience of memory and the persistence of cultural Life. At its core, the exhibition interrogates the historical construction of the body as a site of spectacle, consumption, and amusement. Yet the body presented here refuses these conditions. It is not an object for observation but an accumulation of desires, memories, wounds, and aspirations. It is a thread of hope, a drip of sorrow and joy, and an echo of continuity that persists despite fragmentation. Through these encounters, the exhibition proposes the body as a living archive, one that carries the residues of violence and care, loss and repair, while remaining a space through which alternative narratives of belonging and becoming may emerge.

item.title: Dreamscapes In Transit
item.description: Bag Factory is pleased to present Dreamscapes In Transit, a solo exhibition by Leonardo Sitoe Curated by Muyon Mafulu This exhibition is a result of the Young/Unframed 2026 programme. Dreamscapes in Transit examines the relationship between dreams and the ways in which everyday life shapes and conditions them. Through painting, drawing, and sculpture, Leonardo Sitoe constructs an Afro-surreal world informed by intense and recurring dreams experienced during his daily commute across Johannesburg. Since beginning the routine of travelling between his studio and home, these dreams have become marked by a growing sense of paranoia and uncertainty, reflecting and absorbing the emotional realities of traversing the city’s spatial landscapes and confronting the enduring effects of the Group Areas Act. The exhibition emerges from Sitoe’s ongoing engagement with the changing nature of his dreams and their capacity to absorb, distort, and reconfigure everyday experience. By translating these dream encounters into material form, Dreamscapes in Transit investigates how dreams can function as a connective tissue between individual consciousness and collective memory, while offering alternative ways of understanding identity, place, and belonging within contemporary South Africa.

item.title: How is a triangle the strongest shape?
item.description: How is a triangle the strongest shape? is a musing. The exhibition positions itself as a genuine line of enquiry, taking an interest in the methodology around sustained resistance in the most adversarial of times. Reflecting on the height of the HIV crisis, one wonders how it is that a community experiencing injustice on at least three fronts was able to physically, mentally and spiritually conjure the strength needed for resistance. When compounding Blackness under an Apartheid state, queerness and the intentional neglect of the medical community: where does one draw the strength to extend care to not only themself, but members of their community? As Acts of Care brings to close proximity these difficult histories, How is a triangle the strongest shape? becomes a timely revisiting, and allows itself to be re-sensitized, standing in awe of the leaders before us. With reverence, the question of “how” is truly meant. The exhibition takes particular note of the ephemera associated with resistance. Placards and posters, typically produced in community ahead of demonstrations, are regarded as inadmissible extensions of resistance as a language of their own. As Acts of Care’s third station invites attendees into the practice of this language with the digital and physical production of posters, Latitudes Centre for the Arts becomes a participatory fine art space that engages craft communally. The queer artists of How is a triangle the strongest shape? are invited as expert voices in the practice of tapestry; a practice historically regarded as craft, in a derogatory distinction from fine art. In recognition of this, there is also the recognition of textile works as being historically women led (or relegated?) mediums of production. Through this gendered lens, the exhibition simultaneously pays homage to the lesbian community’s unforgettable role as both carer and advocate at the height of the HIV/AIDS crisis. The collapse of this patriarchal-colonial distinction makes room for something or someone else. In consideration of the exhibition’s titular question, one might find the answer in simultaneously asking: why is L the first letter in LGBTIQ+? Both mythological and autobiographical vivid portraiture act as a visual reminder of the very thing that might make endurance possible within marginalized communities: the community itself.

item.title: TO SWALLOW HOT COALS
item.description: Our family album was always an enigma, tucked away in my mother’s bedroom. My parents divorced when I was 9 years old, and most of what I know about my father comes from the photographs my mother kept and stories from those who knew him. We rarely spoke of him, yet my father remained a titular ghost, looming over us, uninvited. My father is a soil scientist. I became a horticulturist. When I finally encountered the archive, I expected it to mirror what I carried: rage, hurt, a haunting absence. Instead I found birthdays, weddings, honeymoons and portraits of family and friends since forgotten. This archive refused my feelings. In their place came a different confusion, why had my mother kept these at all, these images of a man who had chosen not to stay? The grief sent me looking, not with any clear method, but with the instinct of a child given a colouring book with half the pages missing, pressing colour into the outlines. I turned these documents over, looking for the seams in the family so carefully composed. I began to cut up, paint over and paint in these photographs,because a photograph insists it is the whole of what happened, and these were not. These new compositions do not offer a resolution. Instead, they offer an account of a life lived in the gap between the recorded and the withheld. I began making my own photographs to inhabit the blank pages my mother left behind, using the camera to claim the years that fell through the physical album. Each composition serves as a site where her mythography and my lived experience are held together: unresolved but reconciled. We continue to construct fictions. It is the necessary architecture of how to live.

item.title: If you tear the paper, the ship will sink.
item.description: Artist Statement Kyra Papé Holz is an abstract artist working with fluid mediums. She explores form and its disruption through drawing, painting, printmaking and sculpture. Her interests are in the boundaries or non-boundaries that are being pushed, destabilised, or contained. Her practice is a response to her personal, emotional, and physical material experiences. “I would simply like to move through the chaos, to find moments of peace, to find balance." Her work shifted after experiencing traumatic losses and moved towards an exploration of peaceful chaos. While maintaining her exploration of disrupted boundaries, she also explores the ebb and flow of the human experience in an abstract way. Her practice is deeply rooted in the dichotomies of existence, in the fragility of change, and in the reality of impermanence. “If you tear the paper, the ship will sink.” - alludes to the ideas of disruption, balance and fragility. It is human nature to crave a sense of understanding, whether the answers are accessible or not. In her capacity, Papé Holz tries to make sense of the chaos of life through her abstract artworks. In her process, she visualises control and repetition co-existing with fluid and free mark-making. Her work does not intend to display difference, rather she explores the blurring of the boundary. "I work intuitively, the ink and I play, dance and get lost. I don't like to work with any preconceived ideas; I allow myself the freedom to make. While some works and I may battle others are simpler to make. I may not always have the words to express what I want to say, but my art is my language, my way of making sense of the world, and my experience of it."

item.title: Face(t)s of The City
item.description: In the 35th year of its existence, the Bag Factory presents a solo exhibition featuring the cofounder and resident artist, Kagiso Patrick Mautloa, curated by Ntshadi Mofokeng. His expansive artistic practice and convivial nature are embedded in the very fabric of this community. Having been a resident of Johannesburg from infancy, he has borne witness to every iteration of its physical, social and clamorous personality over the past seven decades. His considered engagement with the city manifests across drawings, layered paintings, multimedia collages, and his iconic sculptures. In his own words, “I find inspiration from the inner city of Johannesburg where found objects are collected both consciously and unconsciously. In the studio, they are given new life through the transformative process of art-making.”

item.title: Site Forming: where encounter takes form
item.description: Site Forming: where encounter takes form brings together Swaline Mkhonto and Zovuyo Pendu, the 2025/2026 recipients of the Young Womxn Studio Bursary, founded and funded by artist and Bag Factory alum Sam Nhlengethwa. After almost a year working side by side in the studios, the exhibition reflects an ongoing encounter between two practices, one turning toward the external and the physicality of geology, the other toward the interior landscape of the self. Both artists are drawn to the duality of the fixed and the fluid, yet each arrives there differently. Mkhonto’s installation takes its cues from Tsitsi Dangarembga’s novel Nervous Conditions and from Makhololo in Eswatini. Dreaming, weather, sight/site and memory are translated through her signature printed silks, alongside sculpture, video, text and collaborative research. Pendu’s large-scale paintings ask how the psyche navigates seemingly opposing notions of self. Rather than resting in the contradiction of binary thinking, her work opens space for new possibilities to emerge. At the heart of the exhibition is the idea that a site is not something fixed, but something continually becoming. Form here is not the act of holding on to what has been encountered; it is a constant state of alteration through encounter. Viewers are invited to bear witness to the work, and to notice how their own presence and interaction act upon them in turn. This reflexivity is central to the experience the artists have crafted. Collaboration shaped the making of the exhibition, both inside and beyond the studio, reflecting the value of an artist community in a field that can otherwise be isolating. Pendu invited curator Penina Chalumbira into her process, while Mkhonto deepened her work with the Letsema collective: Nthabiseng Mofokeng, Mbako Moemise and Eva Rose London. A series of public programmes will follow the opening, offering deeper engagement with the exhibition’s concepts and the artists’ processes. Details will be announced on Bag Factory Artists’ Studios social media and mailing list. This exhibition is made possible by Sam Nhlengethwa and Bag Factory Artists’ Studios, with support from the National Arts Council.

item.title: What’s in the Bag?
item.description: What’s in the Bag? Curated by Ntshadi Mofokeng First presented at: Momentum Aardklop 2026 Venue: NWU Gallery, Potchefstroom Exhibition dates: 29 September – 3 October 2026 For 35 years, Bag Factory Artists’ Studios has fostered collaboration, co-learning and experimentation. From its humble building in Newtown, Johannesburg, its reach extends across the globe. As a meeting point for artists, curators and art writers across generations, disciplines, styles and thematic concerns, Bag Factory nurtures and accelerates artistic careers, leaving an indelible mark on the cultural landscape of the city and the country. What’s in the Bag? brings together current studio artists and recent residency artists, offering a broad spectrum of techniques, approaches and ideas that reflect the dynamism of their practices. The exhibition is a presentation of works readily available for display, reflecting recent activity within the studios. On any given day, one might hear the knocking of a hammer as a work is framed, the splash of brushes being rinsed of luminous colour, the hushed exchange of ideas, and the familiar musical selections that soundtrack the creative process. This sustained attention to the labour of artmaking is evident in the distinct gestures and approaches of each artist. The exhibition encompasses paper-based drawings and prints, oil and acrylic paintings on canvas, and works incorporating rust on steel. It offers a glimpse into the diverse and often multidisciplinary practices that shape the Bag Factory community. Featured Artists The exhibition features: Gail Behrmann, Erla Haraldsdóttir, Sharlene Khan, Candice Kramer, LL Editions, Kagiso Pat Mautloa, Andrew Murray, Richard “Specs” Ndimande, Levy Pooe and Joe Turpin. They are joined by recipients of Bag Factory’s signature awards programmes, which support the development and professional growth of emerging artists: Young Womxn Studio Bursary 2025/2026: Swaline Mkhonto and Zovuyo Pendu Young/Unframed 2026: Mosa Anita Kaiser and Leonardo Sitoe Cassirer Welz Award 2025: Smiso Cele The thread of peer learning and intergenerational exchange connects these artists, reflecting Bag Factory’s enduring legacy of artistic collaboration and knowledge-sharing across decades. About Bag Factory Artists’ Studios Bag Factory Artists’ Studios is a Johannesburg-based visual arts organisation celebrating its 35th anniversary in 2026. Established in 1991, the organisation has made a significant contribution to the development of contemporary visual art in South Africa. Bag Factory provides studio space and professional development opportunities for artists, curators and writers at different stages of their careers. Its programmes include exhibitions, open studios, workshops, awards, mentorship initiatives, and international artist and curator residencies. The organisation has cultivated a cross-generational community in which emerging and established practitioners work alongside one another, exchange ideas and develop their practices. Its distinguished alumni include co-founder David Koloane, Sam Nhlengethwa, Mmakgabo Helen Sebidi, Bongi Dhlomo-Mautloa, Penny Siopis, Lady Skollie, Blessing Ngobeni and Bronwyn Katz.

item.title: Kindred
item.description: To look beyond the limitations of the human figure, which have been echoed in structures of representation across the globe, Kindred moves us away from the familiar figure of the human form, calling upon artists to explore the other-worldly through their distinct practices in an effort to dismantle how we see and make sense of the world and what it means to inhabit our skin. For centuries, human exceptionalism has put us at the apex of what is living simultaneously, creating exclusionary practices of defining the proper perception of what it means to be an individual. Western enlightenment positioned the white man as the exemplar of civilisation, with everyone else seen as peripheral and secondary existence. What would it mean to dismantle these hierarchies and rethink regimes of representations that help us make sense of the world. What can foreign forms teach us about what we consider familiar and why. The speculative, which is intrinsically linked to other-worlding, has shown itself to be a generative practice that helps us journey beyond present times and present configurations, testing the limit of how familiar the foreign can actually be. The speculative is an area which allows for less documented, marginalised and underrepresented modes of being to enjoy unadulterated exploration not hampered by real-life conventions. To speculate is to dream and to allow what would be considered strange to lie up closely beside you in an effort to make sense of the world and the futures we are constructing. Julia Kristeva puts words to this quite succinctly, reminding us that the uncanny allows for the foreign to push up against the familiar in an effort to examine that which we wish to expel from the human form and, in turn, examine our vulnerabilities and limitations as a society. Some artists like Lionel Mbayiwa pull from a very real and ancestral place, their figures and creatures inspired by indigenous oral storytelling. They then speculate from this archive and create worlds where their stories can be engaged with in this contemporary moment. Other artists like Liam Van der Heever and Oupa Sibeko create a parallel world based on our existing one where the human condition can be unravelled to a point of no recognition. The uncanny lives true in Van Der Heever’s sculptures, which take a recognisable object like dominoes and fuse materially with a foreign household object like the dishwashing sponge, making commentary on the power of play whilst simultaneously interrogating generational trauma. Sibeko, on the other hand, creates these abstract creatures through frottage and his close relationship with the real streets of Cape Town, from which he picks up the surface in his pastel works, divorcing us from any point of recognition of the source, which in this case is the street itself. When reaching this point of no recognition in what we see these artists open up the space to address the intangible like social dynamics, political upheaval and human plight. This exploration of other worlds must go beyond just the figurative or the creature, but should also include the strangely familiar that artists reach in the creation of space or mood. For artists like Hanna Noor Mahomed, with a practice heavily embedded in the abstract, the environment is created through productive ambiguity, space, and colour all mingling to create hushed moods and symbolic moments that engage certain political or social statements. On the other hand, Stodel attempts to use the foreign in order to find the familiar by using found images and archive to collage a sense of home, building environments that can become a transgressive act of homing. For some of these artists, like Stodel, Mahomed, and Sibeko, the figure is nowhere to be seen. However, a room, a forest, or an abstract space of shapes disturbs what we may consider as foreign to the self or familiar to our bodies. Other worlds in this case become an imaginative means to refigure how we see our surroundings and possibly fill in the gaps where reality just cannot muster. The strangely familiar is engaged with in a wide variety of ways. For some it is more of a direct confrontation with the depiction of otherworldly creatures. For others, the strangely familiar takes on an uncanny flavour as we explore what wants to be expelled or what could be defined as abject. Sibeko yet again is a testament to this as his frottage traces the neglected streets that made up District Six littered with potholes that then become these attractive playful figures. He explores what has been forgotten, displaced, or disregarded through performative play and gesture. For artists like Ande Magoso, the human and the creature become intermingled as they explore hybridity and dualism through their own heritage being Xhosa and Zulu. Donna Haraway’s cyborgian theory shows how the exploration of such hybridity, which destabilises the human, allows us to begin to think of more expansive ways of being and identities that step outside of the normative construction of the human. Sadiya Hartman’s critical fabulation, which calls for the need to speculate where there is erasure within certain marginalised histories, is pertinent within this group of artists. This juncture between speculation and restoration builds another world where Blackness and other fringe identities attached to our ontological form are seen to be free, safe to embody, elastic in its aesthetics, and all-encompassing in its unapologetic nature. Lionel Mbayiwa invigorates traditional Shona oral storytelling using symbolic tropes of animals like the fish and the bird to make commentary on contemporary issues like political leadership in A Broken Nation (2025) and modern-day surveillance in Pasi Pamera Ziso (2024). Another example of critical fabulation is Ande Magoso’s uNomadonsa, where he takes the historical accounts of uNonggqawuza and the cattle killings movement of 1856 and decides to speculate and insert a figure who was a witness to the moment, bringing in a different perspective. Scientific and traditional forms of knowledge often position other-worlding and the speculative within mysticism or other fields that fall outside formal analytical approaches to humanity and ontology. Yet speculation is, at its core, a mode of knowledge production: a process in which the event itself becomes a site of inquiry, generating possible futures while revealing where we are situated as communities and where we wish to direct our collective trajectories. Other-worlding that releases the human figure as the centre allows for expansive thinking that brings in new possibilities that could be helpful to understanding the realities we live in. Speculation or other-worlding is therefore not rooted in naivety, toxic positivity, or an unwavering investment in individual advancement and material success. The speculative can instead offer a means of excavating the obscured truths of life, drawing on histories and realities that may unsettle us, produce unfamiliar perspectives, and compel us to interrogate the true limitations of what it means to be human and what it means to occupy certain communities and earth. item.title: Inherited Forms
item.description: Inherited Forms brings together the practices of five Ugandan women artists whose work explores how material knowledge, memory and cultural inheritance move across generations and into contemporary forms of making. At the centre of the exhibition is the Ugandan mat, or omukeeka, as a point of departure for thinking about inheritance as an active process. A mat carries knowledge through its materials, patterns and techniques, as well as through the people, relationships and communities involved in its making. What happens when an inherited form moves into another material, another context or another generation? What remains, what changes, and what becomes possible? The exhibition begins with Keerera Nellie’s photographs of the Karibu Project, documenting women artisans engaged in the traditional practice of mat-making. Her images draw attention to the materials, gestures and relationships through which cultural knowledge is shared and transmitted. This lineage continues through the work of the participating artists. Olivia Mary Nantongo uses the traditional woven mat as a canvas and reflective surface, combining acrylic paint, oil pastels, foreign and repurposed objects to explore identity and relationships. Darren Akoragye draws from childhood memories of her grandmother’s mat, reimagining its physical form through digital landscapes. Laruni Diana Mary transforms maize husks into sculptural forms and masks, while Namala Olivia works with raffia and banana fibre to create sculptures inspired by everyday Ugandan life. Together, the works bring craft-based materials and knowledge into contemporary artistic practices, creating new relationships between inherited forms, materials and ideas. Inherited Forms considers what happens when craft enters contemporary art and how this changes the way we understand both. Craft carries histories of skill, material knowledge, labour and community, yet its place within contemporary art and collecting continues to evolve. The exhibition invites viewers to encounter these materials as part of a living artistic practice and to consider their place within the future of art collecting. As artists continue to reinterpret inherited materials through sculpture, photography, painting and digital practice, craft can be understood as a continuing source of contemporary artistic knowledge, with the capacity to shape how future collections represent culture, material history and artistic practice. item.title: Retrieve
item.description: Retrieve is a group show bringing together artists whose work turns away from the spectacle of crisis and toward something closer: the interior lives and spaces inside it. This exhibition visualises the softness, quiet, exhaustion, and weight of respite within melancholic times. Writing about the emotional condition of our present moment, critic Vamika Sinha reaches for a term coined by Sri Lankan artist Abdul Halik Azeez: melancholy, to describe not a temporal state, like the now-familiar postcolonial or neocolonial, but an experiential one — the stupefying affect of living in a world still functioning on imperialist capitalist logics, and watching it self-cannibalise into collapse. It is a feeling, Sinha writes, that is "oddly universal, uniting in its thick, clotting grief." Retrieve begins here, inside that thickness of grief, and erects a spatial dimension for that melancholy to be investigated, meditated on, and made visible. What does it look like to sit with a grief we are expected to ignore, in a time of extreme censorship and disempowerment, and of extreme reactiveness, when everything demands an instant response? In his 1931 review-essay "Linke Melancholie" (left-wing melancholy), Walter Benjamin took aim at the poets of his own defeated left. They had, he argued, turned political disappointment into a cultural commodity: a melancholy that mistook the shape of loss for a politics, possessing its grief rather than risking it for something unproven. Faced with fascism, he judged this melancholy, disabling. It paralysed artists and writers when it should have propelled them to speak, or to make new language. But his target was melancholy as a posture, a stance struck in public and commodified as an identity. Retrieve proposes a reposturing, or rather a slouching: a melancholy that lies down, rests, leans in, and curls up.Here grief is not opposed to action. It is the daily labour of living with what has been lost, and it may even be where political attention begins. Grief is the imprint left where love once lived, or perhaps love itself at another point in its life cycle, it informs our orientations. Grief lingers between rooms like winter sun, and stays when we're not home. This show pays careful attention to the home, not as shelter or an exceptional individual experience, but rather as the site where this grief is most intimately felt, rearranged, and lived with. It then follows that grief outward into public space and the natural world, where humans and non-humans share it. In times where we are made hyper-aware of massive catastrophes, genocides, ecological despair and powerlessness in real time, and expected to carry on, to work as usual, to ignore, to enjoy and hope regardless, these works make room for what we are often deprived of. Melancholy speaks to a condition of our times: we carry this grief, and we remain moved, affected both directly and in witness to open wounds. The title names the show's gesture: to recover something taken. Rest, beauty, and exhaustion locate the pain and recover our ability to sit with melancholy, through the interior life and the desire to recoup. item.title: Drafts of the future.
item.description: Drafts of the Future investigates a deceptively simple question: How does the future come into existence? The exhibition begins from the proposition that the future does not suddenly arrive. Before it manifests, it is continuously imagined, inherited, experienced and constructed through three interconnected states: memory, presence and speculation. Memory is where we begin. It is the archive of what has already happened: the places we grew up in, the people who shaped us, the objects we remember, the spaces that hold emotional residue, and the histories we inherit before we have the language to name them. Memory is not simply a record of the past. It is an active force that continues to shape how we understand ourselves and the worlds we inhabit. The second movement is presence, or being. This is the space of the now: what we experience, desire, negotiate and become in the present. The decisions we make today, the relationships we form, the identities we inhabit and the conditions in which we live are all contributing to the person and society we are becoming. The final movement is speculation, or becoming. Here, the exhibition turns towards what has not yet arrived. We imagine, hope, question and project. We carry the lessons of our histories and the realities of our present into possible futures. In doing so, we do not simply wait for the future. We draft it. The works in Drafts of the Future therefore operate as fragments of a larger temporal conversation. They move between domestic spaces, childhood, cultural memory, inherited knowledge, identity, womanhood, belonging, labour, grief, selfhood and transformation. Together, they ask what it means to inherit a past while actively participating in the creation of something that does not yet exist. The exhibition proposes that the future is not a blank page. It is a document already be. VIEW THE FULL SHOW : https://canva.link/ao42ubk5nypduo9

item.title: What We Carry: A Viewpoint of Liminal Existence
item.description: What we carry brings together six artists to consider identity as something continuously formed through inheritance, memory, movement and lived experience. Across these practices the past does not remain behind us. it is carried through bodies, objects, language, food, images, relationships and material. Sometimes inheritance is immediately visible; at other Times it survives as a trace. may be obscured, fragmented, transformed or felt without being fully known. The exhibition occupies the space between what is received and what is remade: between ancestry and self- authorship, remembering and forgetting, belonging and becoming. Rather than understanding reclamation as a return to an untouched past, what we carry considers it an active relationship with inheritance. what we receive may be preserved, questioned transformed or refused. We inherit, we carry, we remake or sometimes even refuse. VIEW THE FULL SHOW : https://canva.link/8cirocmi42j08ct

item.title: meeting you where you are
item.description: A line, a mark, a piece of fabric, an image or a word can feel familiar because we have encountered it before. How much can we know about another person through what they create? And what happens in the space between what an artwork offers us and what we bring to it? meeting you where you are considers the relationships that develop between artists, artworks, and viewers. Bringing together practices from three artists who explore marks, repetition, writing-like forms, and accumulation. The exhibition begins with the curiosity that arises when an artwork seems to communicate something without making itself entirely legible. Rather than looking for a single visual language across the works, the exhibition explores how meaning changes through the act of looking, and what happens in the space between recognition and understanding. I have found myself reading these works through the lens of text, even when text is not necessarily what they are concerned with. These are not necessarily statements about the artists’ intentions. They are my own ways of engaging with the artworks, shaped by my particular interests and experiences. The works hold traces of their makers. Marks gather, patterns emerge, and gestures reveal moments of stopping, returning, and beginning again. These traces offer glimpses into an artwork's life, but they do not necessarily explain it. An artwork may change as an artist returns to it, or remain physically unchanged while the people encountering it see something different each time. Artworks meet us through different forms of encounter. I see time accumulating in Cathy Abraham’s marks, residue in Kganya Malatjie’s almost-legible forms and obscurity in Luncedo Phillip’s dimmed paintings. An artwork's physical dimension does not neecessarily determine the significance it will hold for us, just as an image cannot fully prepare us for the experience of encountering the work in person. Rather than offering a single way to interpret the works, meeting you where you are makes space for shifting impressions. It asks us to pay attention to what we notice, what we assume, and what might change when we encounter an artwork again. The work may be different, we may be different, or both may remain as they were. Explore Catalogue Here: https://www.canva.com/design/DAHZMo2d25E/Ir5bBbVZa6P1wbNL_STucw/edit

item.title: To Fold a Line
item.description: To Fold a Line brings together eight artists associated with the Nsukka School who extend line beyond drawing through their handling of material. Working through folding, weaving, coiling, binding, carving, incising, and painting, they turn line into a visual language that engages material memory, contemporary identity, and thought. Here, to fold a line is not necessarily to bend it. It is to make line enter material, emerge through the connection and arrangement of materials, occupy space, acquire volume, and generate new relationships. Here, line is woven, painted onto fibre, bound, carved into wood, excavated as grooves, and built up from discarded materials. Across these varied approaches, line moves beyond the surface and becomes a physical presence. Rooted in the experimental legacy of the Nsukka School, these artists extend an approach to line that draws on Indigenous visual traditions, where line, pattern, incision, and geometry have long served as aesthetic and communicative languages. From Igbo Uli to Ndebele geometric mural art, Yolŋu Rarrk, Māori Kōwhaiwhai, and Whakairo, line and linear structures have taken diverse cultural and material forms. To Fold a Line considers how artists have broadened the horizon of how lines can be created, encountered, and understood in art. The exhibition also draws from the philosophy of Igwebuike (“strength in multitude”), in which individual elements gain greater presence and force through coming together as a whole. In this exhibition, materials, lines, fragments, gestures, and forms are similarly brought together to create complex wholes. What may appear ordinary or insignificant in isolation acquires new meaning through the artist’s intentionality and process. Rather than presenting the Nsukka School as a fixed historical movement, To Fold a Line positions it as an evolving collective that encourages experimentation while remaining grounded in local knowledge systems. The exhibition asks how seemingly simple ideas, forms, and materials can be transformed, manipulated, and reorganised into complex wholes. item.title: The Weight of Distance
item.description: The Weight of Distance examines connections between Africa, Portugal and Brazil shaped by colonialism, migration, displacement and cultural exchange. Bringing Anglophone and Lusophone histories into dialogue, the exhibition considers the lasting effects of Portuguese colonialism within wider African histories. Taking Atlantic continuity as its point of departure, the exhibition explores how cultural knowledge, beliefs, memories and identities move across the Atlantic, transforming through displacement and exchange. The Atlantic is understood not as a seamless connection, but as a space marked by rupture, movement and persistence, where histories, languages, beliefs and forms of knowledge have been carried, adapted and reconstituted across generations. . The exhibition considers distance as more than geographical separation. It can fracture relationships between places, generations and histories, while also creating new forms of connection and belonging. It asks how histories remain present when displaced, transformed or excluded from dominant narratives, and how memory is shaped through cultural transmission, lived experience and place. The Weight of Distance moves through two interconnected themes: Atlantic Continuities and Making Home. Atlantic Continuities — Beré Magalhães, Benigino Mangovo and Eunice Pais — explores ancestry, spirituality, ecology and cultural memory. Their works consider how inherited knowledge, beliefs and histories persist across generations while acquiring new meanings through changing places and contexts. Making Home — Débora Sandjai, Mário Macilau, Queila Fernandes and Beatriz Manteigas — considers belonging, displacement and relationships to place. Through the body, portraiture, landscape and lived environments, the artists explore how identity and notions of home are shaped by movement, memory and experience. Presented through Latitudes Online as part of the RMB Latitudes and Art School Africa CuratorLab, The Weight of Distance brings diverse geographical and historical perspectives into conversation. The exhibition uses the digital space to bring geographically dispersed practices into proximity. Here, distance becomes both subject and method: the separation between places becomes a way of thinking about what connects them. **To view the full publication online, including interviews with participating artists and additional material, please follow the link provided in the catalogue. item.title: The Present As...
item.description: It seems like African contemporaneity is often imagined, talked about, and conceived as moving in between one thing and the other. Its histories (broadly addressed as pre- and during colonialism) and its future (there was not long ago a raving excitement of afrofuturism), between geographies (an here and a there) and inevitably between cultures (a local and a global), between identities (afropolitan, global citizen, cosmopolitan, yoruba, Swahili), and between political states, economic fluxes, and spiritual understanding of self. Speaking of the future, writer and curator Bonaventure Soh Bejeng Ndikung at the 2015 African Future Festival, Johannesburg (later published as African Futures: Thinking about the future in word and image) asked; “What is this sudden interest in futurism and the future, especially related to the African continent but also globally? I have been asking myself what is behind it... Is there a possibility that he [we] kept on talking about the future to evade talking about the present? My point is this: what are we trying to skip in not talking about the present, and not talking about the past?” This exhibition asks what is to be found in considering the present as is; beyond a portal to the past and a springboard for the future - a dense, active space where histories, futures, identities, commodities, bodies, and geographies coexist? What's in the present beyond memories of the past, and ideas and directions for the future? The Present As… Movement For one, the present is characterised by movement. As the multidisciplinary artist Emeka Okereke says, the story of Africa is one of journeys. Indeed, Africa and Africans are constantly journeying; moving and becoming mutable. Using movement as one such proposition of constituencies of the present within the larger exhibition, viewers are invited to consider the popular, inexpensive, Chinese-made plastic weave bag as an icon par excellence indexing migration; the conditions that necessitate it, the conditions it creates and the potentialities that it holds for the future. As a marker for the transnational, global, intra and intercontinental movement of Africans in the present, the exhibition invites the artists to respond to the bags, well known to Africans and the globe at large through mimicking, extensions, reimagination, subversion or activation. It asks the artists to consider the histories of the plastic bag, its functionalities, relationships contained within it, and its several representations for the present. The bag is known by different names across the world, often through names that associate it with working-class, migrant, or refugee communities. In Nigeria, it is called “Ghana Must Go,” a recalling of the 1983 exile of Ghanaian nationals from the country. In the UK, it is called Bangladeshi Bag, reflective of Bangladeshi immigrants. In Germany, it is called the Türkenkoffer (Turkish suitcase). It is called Chinaman tote in America, the Amah bag in Hong Kong, the Guyanese Samsonite in the Caribbean, the Shangaan or Zimbabwe Bag in South Africa, and Osuofia in Kenya/Uganda. However, regardless of the representative names of the bag that suggest migration, refugeeship, and survival, it is found in many African homes as storage materials. In the NoViolet Bulawayo's “We Need New Names” fashion, both continental, diaspora and global creative entities from Obinna Obioma, Phoebe Philo to Balenciaga have also made efforts to appropriate or reclaim the bag. The bag is evocative of migratory histories and present, rapid movements and continuous settlements, purported disposability of African bodies within global trends, resituationships, geopolitical and economic struggles of the working class. It therefore serves as a starting point through which the exhibition considers the present as a space of simultaneous and sometimes contradictory conditions: movement and staying, utility and aesthetics, stigma and value, individuality and collectivity, locality and circulation. The artists are invited to consider what can emerge from these conditions. Another proposition for the present includes The Present as… a condition in which the present is considered beyond its temporal understandings but manifested as a complex intersection of physical geopolitical, globalised, technological, cross cultural and infrastructural realities. Other propositions include the present as… a site of inquiry, the present as… a site of expression, etc. The exhibition leaves the present as an open-ended space where further propositions can be generated. The Present As… proposes the present as a field that is continually encountered and reformulated; as movement, condition, expression, inquiry, memory, labour, desire, pleasure, contradiction, or otherwise. These propositions alongside many others overlap, contradict and remain open to further articulation through the works themselves. Bringing together artists working across painting, mixed media, installation and sculpture, The Present As considers the simultaneous constancy and mutability of the present. The exhibiting artists include Tochukwu Orazulike, Wisdom Uche, Putin Ofori Bempong, Joseph Kojo Hoggar, Paulcy Odama, Snelihle Maphumulo, and Oluchi Anaghoba. Wisdom Uche contrasts notions of family with the encroaching reality of solitude that symptomises our contemporaneity. Combining figurative style with neoexpressionism, and having the postured body with a palette of whimsical emoticons for a face, the works leave us to contemplate and infer the implied dispositions and relationships of the portrayed figures. Interested in disrupting certainty, Tochukwu Orazulike ruptures the unknowability of the future [no one knows tomorrow] by presenting today as its own distinct orchestra of enigmas. In two of the works in the show, the artist acknowledges a current that has led to the present while asking urgently and poignantly “Where do we go from here?” The bag, an allegory for potential continuous mobility of the present remains closed, inscrutable to us. Finding purpose for archival materials often marked for destruction or abandoned, combining layered images with organic matter, paint and locally sourced materials, Putin Ofori Bempong becomes an inquisitor for the future, investigating, revealing, and reporting the present’s complicity in the destruction of the future. Among swaths of debates and discourses regarding cultural originaries, authenticities and appropriation, Joseph Kojo Hoggar’s installation “Material Study II” uses African wax prints to consider the mobility, intersection, blending and blurring of cultures and identities into a hybrid entities sometimes difficult to fractionalise into distinct originaries. This hybrid bonding is further complicated and intensified by current global circuits of trade, trans and cross cultural exchange and cyberspace communication and conduits. Paulcy Odama’s work is rooted in reflexive inquisition about the notions of self which are constructed by deliberate rubrics and subconscious structures within which childhood has been lived and experienced. Combining materials such as earth, clay, charcoal, paint, and gauze, Odama uses the fundamental human experience of play to explore imbibed systems, ideas and philosophies that continue to bear significance to present being and life. Inioluwa Aboluwarin’s works between new stories that takes inspiration from current mundane realities and historical events, moving fluidly between true life, fantasies, and myths derived from a multiplicity of geographies as he reimagines them in the present and casts his cultural sensibilities and alignments onto them. Snelihle Maphumulo’s work carries the poignant potential for transformation of the symbolism of materials. Working with materials such as cow and sheep hide which she cuts, laser engraves and layers within an installation based practice, she moves from the traditional, ancestral and inherited to the signification of her Christian faith. The work recalls the importance of the material iconography with both belief systems and the contain tensions between both. Her practice is a continuous negotiation of inheritance and new possibilities as identity, belief and belonging unfurls. Oluchi Anaghoba’s submission revolves around the ethnoreligious conflicts she experienced growing up and the continued occurrence of the violence. Although she has since moved, she reflects on the persistence of violent landscapes and its affect on memory and the psyche across time and geographies. item.title: The Body Remembers The Earth
item.description: The Body Remembers the Earth emerged as I considered the idea of a shared memory or consciousness between ourselves and the land, and the ways we can attempt to access it. Returning home to Uganda earlier this year made me more aware of this idea and forced me to consider what might happen if we cannot learn from the land. Perhaps that’s why we are so stagnant, why we are trapped in a cycle of extraction and exploitation across the continent, because we fail to pause and remember the stories of the earth. The exhibition, therefore, asks what it might mean to move beyond simply remembering acts of violence and to actively attempt to repair damaged relationships. Healing, in this context, cannot be separated from the land. If the earth has been wounded through systems of dispossession, then caring for it becomes part of caring for ourselves and the communities that depend upon it. By recognizing the earth as something we are connected to rather than something we possess, the exhibition proposes that healing the land can also become a form of collective healing. Ultimately, this allows us to acknowledge the wounds of colonial history while creating the conditions to grow beyond them. Wahu-Mũchiri’s research demonstrates how landscapes carry political and ideological meanings, revealing that questions of land are inseparable from questions of power, history, and belonging. Mbembe’s work allows us to consider how the violence of colonialism continues to shape the present rather than existing only as a historical event. The violence that occurs on land remains visible in its soil, ecosystems, borders, resources, and in the communities that continue to inhabit it. The body similarly becomes a site of accumulation, carrying histories that are inherited across generations. Land and body, therefore, mirror one another, both holding memories of what has been endured and what continues to shape the present. To sustainably grow and heal, we need to move past the nostalgic haze when considering our relationship to the earth. Instead, it asks how the memories held within land and body can help us imagine decolonial futures. By recognizing the earth as something we are connected to rather than something we possess, the exhibition proposes that healing the land can also become a form of collective healing. Ultimately, this allows us to acknowledge the wounds of colonial history while creating the conditions to grow beyond them. item.title: Material Witness
item.description: The built environment is often understood as a testament to permanence. Buildings, roads, bridges and other forms of infrastructure are designed to resist time, to impose order upon the landscape and to project stability into the future. Yet every constructed form is subject to transformation. Concrete fractures, steel oxidises, timber expands and contracts, paint peels, vegetation takes root in neglected surfaces and architecture slowly absorbs the traces of weather, occupation, maintenance, and abandonment. Rather than existing outside of nature, the built environment remains in constant dialogue with it. Material Witness proposes that these processes should not be understood simply as signs of decline or failure. Instead, they reveal the temporal lives of materials. The exhibition approaches weathering as an ongoing condition through which architecture records its encounters with environmental forces, human intervention and the passage of time. In doing so, it shifts attention away from the ideal of the pristine building and towards the dynamic, unfinished life of the constructed world. Bringing together the work of Kamyar Bineshtarigh, Damon Botha, Lesego Forbes, Michele Mathison, Silindokuhle Shandu, Guy Simpson, Brigitta Stone-Johnson, Kirsty Tinkler, Cathy Xiao and Khanya Zibaya. The exhibition explores the built environment as a site of continual negotiation between permanence and impermanence. Although each artist employs a distinct visual language and material approach, their practices share an attentiveness to the changing conditions of architecture and urban landscape. Their works observe surfaces that have been marked by exposure, structures that bear the evidence of use and adaptation, and environments where natural and human processes intersect. Together, they reveal the built environment not as a collection of static forms but as an evolving material ecology. Underlying the exhibition is the proposition that materials possess their own temporalities. Buildings are not completed when construction ends; they continue to change through weather, maintenance, repair, erosion, occupation, and neglect. Rust, cracks, stains, dust, and improvised interventions are not merely signs of deterioration but records of these ongoing transformations. They testify to architecture's capacity to accumulate histories, making visible the slow and often imperceptible processes through which the world is continually remade. To weather is not simply to deteriorate; it is to endure through transformation. The works assembled in this exhibition suggest that the built environment is best understood not as a finished object but as a living process, continually shaped by material forces that exceed architectural intention. By attending to these slow and often overlooked changes, Material Witness proposes a different way of seeing the spaces we inhabit, one in which time is made visible through matter, and in which the traces of change become evidence not of loss but of the ongoing life of the built world.
